item.research_question: Can bulk high-entropy nitrides (HENs) and carbonitrides (HECNs) be synthesized as single-phase materials, and how do configurational entropy and valence electron concentration (VEC) influence their mechanical properties compared to rule-of-mixtures predictions?
item.material_system: Five bulk HENs (e.g., (CrMoTaVW)N) and four single-phase bulk HECNs (e.g., (CrMoTaVW)CN) synthesized from equiatomic transition metal precursors; HECN #6 and HECN #3 were multi-phase/segregated.
item.processing_route: Hand-mixing of precursor powders (graphite, mononitrides, monocarbides) with 5 at% graphite; high-energy ball milling (SPEX 8000D, 3 hours, WC media, stearic acid, argon); Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) under vacuum (<30 mtorr) at 100 °C/min ramp, 50 MPa pressure, 1 hour hold; Chromium-containing samples sintered at 1600 °C, others at 2200 °C.
item.test_conditions: Nanoindentation using 300 mN force with diamond Berkovich indenter (Oliver and Pharr method); 100 indents per sample spaced 30 µm apart; depth ~800 nm; data filtered for outliers (depth >1400 nm and top/bottom 5%); XRD (Cu K-α) and EDS for phase/chemical analysis.
key_findings: Synthesized 5 single-phase bulk HENs and 4 single-phase bulk HECNs out of 11 total samples prepared.
Hardness of HENs increased by an average of 22% over the rule-of-mixtures (ROM) average of precursors.
Hardness of HECNs increased by an average of 39% over the ROM average of precursors.
Elastic modulus of HENs increased by an average of 17% over ROM values.
Elastic modulus of HECNs increased by an average of 31% over ROM values.
Hardness shows a negative dependence on valence electron concentration (VEC); increasing VEC decreases hardness.
Configurational entropy positively correlates with the increase in hardness over ROM values (entropic strengthening).
HECN #6 exhibited chemical segregation and two major crystal structures (FCC and hexagonal), while HECN #3 showed minor Nb segregation.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the hardness increase to 'entropic strengthening' caused by compositional randomness, where different element sizes induce local strain that impedes dislocation motion. They propose that carbonitrides have higher configurational entropy than nitrides (1.15R vs 0.8R for equiatomic five-metal systems), leading to greater strengthening. Conversely, increasing VEC enhances metallic bond character, which lowers hardness and modulus by allowing atoms to move to local minima rather than cleaving.
item.limitations: The study notes that VEC is an oversimplification for quantifying electronic structure, as mononitrides with equal VEC can have vastly different hardness. Additionally, the Entropy Forming Ability (EFA) descriptor indicates that some compositions (like HECN #3) may require more energetic input to achieve homogeneity. The authors also state they have not determined if the materials are truly entropy-stabilized, as enthalpic contributions and mutual solubility exist.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that purposeful design of configurational entropy and VEC can tune mechanical properties and high-temperature phase stability. They propose that universal adoption of the sublattice model for calculating configurational entropy will bolster the understanding and design of entropy-related properties in high-entropy ceramics.
quotes: The hardness of HENs and HECNs increased by an average of 22% and 39%, respectively, over the rule-of-mixtures average of their monocarbide and mononitride precursors.

This 'entropic strengthening' effect is caused by increased compositional randomness, i.e. the different types and sizes of elements inducing local strain in the lattice which can impede dislocation motion.
Increasing VEC increases metallic bond character and anharmonic lattice vibrations. Therefore, under deformation, the atoms can move to another local minimum structure as opposed to cleaving.
